title: Why is maintaining consistency across frames still so difficult in generated sprite sheets?
author: Historical-Taro-7963
selftext:
I'm working with generated 2D sprite sheets and I keep running into the same problem: **frame-to-frame consistency.**

A single character frame can look fantastic.

Then you ask for a 12-frame walk cycle and things start getting... creative.

Frame 1: perfect character.  
Frame 2: still perfect.  
Frame 3: the sword has apparently become rubber.  
Frame 4: one leg has resigned from the animation and started a new career elsewhere.

Clothes change, proportions drift, weapons deform, silhouettes mutate and sometimes the character seems to age three years between two frames.

The funny part is that every individual image can actually look good.

Then you play the animation.

And suddenly your proud warrior walks like he's trying to remember whether he left the oven on.

The biggest problem I've found is movement itself. Feet don't always alternate correctly, weight transfer can make no sense, and perfectly nice individual poses don't necessarily produce a believable animation when placed in sequence.

So I've started experimenting with a different workflow:

**character appearance → defined key poses → generated frames → manual movement/timing control → cleanup**

Instead of asking the generator to invent the entire animation, I'm trying to separate **appearance from motion**.

My technical question for people actually working with 2D animation and sprite sheets is:

**What workflow are you using to maintain character consistency across a complete animation cycle?**

I'm particularly interested in walk/run cycles, key-pose control, 8-direction animation, weapons/accessories and keeping proportions consistent between frames.

I'm not looking for a magical “MAKE GAME” button. We have enough dangerous buttons already.

I'm interested in workflows that produce something you'd actually be comfortable shipping in a game.

Right now, I'm finding that human eyes and manual cleanup are still doing a surprising amount of the heavy lifting.

Has anyone here found a genuinely better approach?

comments.author: AsparagusOk8818
comments.body:
The best results I have seen use dedicated animation models. To get those results, you need exceptionally clean - and usually very simple - sprites. 

It's just where the technology is at right now. It might get better... it might not.

comments.author: zenmatrix83
comments.body: the problem with llms and image gen is like asking a new person everytime for something, since each person is slightly differently. There really  is nothing that can create 100% consistancy at this time,  generating sprite sheets are better then single images but even each of the frames can have issues. A comprise is a 2.5d sprite, basically do a 3d image animate it, and create a spirte sheet from that use animations. You should possibly feed that into in image gen software to generate a new one with the style you need.

comments.author: KhaosPT
comments.body:
I gave up on sprite generation and video. Video looks great and ar the beginning I had great results. Then the model changed and I'm having bad results on video: video decides to change sprite, instead of walking decides to jump or do a death animation(!) . I eventually just vibe coded a dragonbones eske app that takes the sprite and does the part separation, paper doll style. I had to fiddle to get the animation and cropping right and then it's a native port to godot skeleton. 

No more 8 tries to get some walking sprite sheets. You get the base right once, it's done. It used to require me adjusting the manual cropping of the parts but opus 5.5 dropped and just does it perfectly now. The animations are still fiddly, but I honestly have not tried to fix then with opus 5.5 , most of them I adjusted by hand.
